speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for the Prime Minister I move:
That on Wednesday, February 3, 1954, and every Wednesday thereafter to the end of the session, government notices of motions and government orders shall have precedence over all business except the introduction of bills, questions by members and notices of motions for the production of papers.
I should say by way of explanation that this has completed private members' days, so that-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON WEDNESDAYS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. Before the minister proceeds to discuss the substance of the motion I raise the point as to whether or not it is proper for this motion to be made at this time. I would call Your Honour's attention to citations 132 and 135 in Beauchesne's third edition. Citation 132 is as follows:
The proceedings of the house must be taken up in accordance with the order of business given in the order paper.
83276-109i
And citation 135 states:
The rule which requires a strict adherence to the order paper is absolutely necessary to prevent surprise.
The motion the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Harris) is seeking to move on behalf of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) is found at page 17 of the order paper for today under the heading of government notices of motions, which is a category away at the back of today's order paper.
Today's order of business has already been provided by the rules of the house, and I submit it is not proper to bring this motion forward, ahead of its proper position, and try to move it under the order for motions. I recognize that this has been done on some previous occasions, but it must also be recognized that on some of those occasions I have objected to that course being followed.
Another reference to which I would draw Your Honour's attention is standing order 17 at page 61 of Beauchesne's third edition which reads:
17 (1) All items standing on the orders of the day (except government orders) shall be taken up according to the precedence assigned to each on the order paper.
(2) Whenever government business has precedence, government orders may be called in such sequence as the government may think fit.
It is quite clear, Mr. Speaker, that part (1) of standing order 17 gives the government leeway as to the order in which it calls its orders when the category of government orders is properly before the house. This is reinforced by part (2) of that same standing order which makes it clear that the government has that right to choose the order of its own business, but only when government business has precedence.
If notice of this motion had been given a day or two earlier so that it could have been proposed yesterday, that would have been quite proper, and the house would have considered the matter on its merits. In view of the fact that notice was not given until Monday, it comes on today's order paper in the class which I have indicated, and since this is the first time that this issue has arisen in this parliament it should be settled in the proper manner at this time.
Apart altogether from references to citations and precedents that all of us can give -and some hon. members think I am adept at doing that-it seems to me that plain

Business of the House common sense makes it clear that it is unfair, the order of business for the day having been set out in the order paper, for it to be possible on that day for the government to change the day's order paper by trying to bring forward a motion of this kind. Despite the fact that on some occasions this has been done, and in my view done improperly, I submit it should not be done at this time.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON WEDNESDAYS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it had been my intention to raise this point but I had assumed that the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration recognized the difficulty and was about to explain how he proposed to bring this motion forward. I believe that a very important consideration is raised and that the motion cannot be heard, except by unanimous consent, at this stage of the proceedings. The list of orders is clearly set out in the order paper for today as follows:
Questions; Notices of Motions for the Production of Papers; Notices of Motions; Public Bills and Orders; Government Notices of Motions; Government Orders.
This does not come under "notices of motions". This comes under the clear definition of "government notices of motions", which is the last but one on the order paper today. Questions are set forth; motions for the production of papers are set forth; and then on page 10 we have "notices of motions", which are obviously referred to in the next item in the order of precedence. Then we have "government notices of motions", then following that "public bills and orders", and after that "government notices of motions"- that is, the heading under which this motion is now presented.
The time or the day on which this notice of motion was entered has nothing to do with the question now before us. It appears in its proper place as a government notice of motion not because of the time it was entered with the Clerk but because this is private members' day. It will be seen that in the order of precedence the questions are questions of private members; the notices of motions for the production of papers are notices of private members; the notices of motions are notices by private members; public bills and orders are public bills and orders presented by private members. Only after all the business of the private members has been dealt with do we come to government notices of motions, and under the heading "government notices of motions" on page 17 of the order paper we find one motion, and that is the one now before us.
I submit that the rules are clear, Mr. Speaker, and the practice is clear on the basis of the status of private members'


business in this house and without unanimous consent this motion cannot be called for consideration until the orders appearing before it on the order paper for today have been called and dealt with.

If I may conclude, then I will hear the hon. member. Hon. members seem to question the propriety of the motion being made under "motions". The very citation that the hon. member read, citation 132, is the one that Mr. Speaker Macdonald had to deal with, when on Monday, September 4, 1950, a similar motion was moved by the Prime Minister. I am reading now from the Journals of that day.
A point of order was raised by Mr. Drew, that, as this motion appeared under "government notices of motions" on page 9 of the "order paper", it should not properly come forward for consideration at this time.
He developed this same argument today. Here is the ruling of Mr. Speaker Macdonald:
I may say to the Leader of the Opposition that last year I considered this same question, and it then seemed to me, as he says, that such a motion

should be considered at a later time. But under citation 132 in Beauchesne's second edition I notice the following:
"The motions allowed on routine proceedings are motions relating to the business of the house and for the discussion of reports from committees".
This motion definitely relates to the business of the house and should therefore be considered at this time. I think the misunderstanding arises from the fact that such motions generally appear under "government notices of motions". Actually, however, they are not "government notices of motions" in the usual sense.
In view of the citation which I have mentioned in Beauchesne's second edition and of the practice which has been established, I think the motion should be considered now.
Later in 1951 a similar situation arose and Mr. Speaker Macdonald ruled-and I am quoting from page 290 of the Journals of Monday, December 10, 1951-
Mr. Speaker ruled that, as the proposed motion dealt with the business of the house and was not a "government notice of motion" in the usual sense, it was in order at this time and that he had previously so ruled on Monday, September 4, 1950, when a similar point of order had been raised.
This I would say is a proper view of the situation. I do not think there could be any argument that would make me change my decision to accept the previous rulings of Mr. Speaker Macdonald on the point which I think are very sound.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a member rising after such a clear indication of Your Honour's present opinion must appear to have a certain amount of temerity; nevertheless, since you have issued a cordial invitation, may I take a moment or two to express a different view.
I start, sir, with this premise, which I would ask you to consider carefully. I think it was yesterday, or it may have been the day before, that you indicated to the house you would be prepared under certain circumstances to undertake a review of a ruling made by a previous Speaker in connection with the rights of members or leaders of parties to ask questions or to make statements after statements made by ministers.
I draw attention to that fact only to ask you, if when you are prepared to review a ruling of a former Speaker on one matter, whether you should consider also the possibility of reviewing, and if necessary revising, a ruling by a former Speaker on another matter. I say that because I admit at the outset that the ruling of Mr. Speaker Macdonald, if accepted, would be a clear precedent against the point of view I now put forward.
I admit that in fact we are asking you to review that ruling, but I submit that there are good grounds upon which that request can be made. I shall not rehearse the grounds
Business of the House
covered by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) or by my leader, but I would ask you to consider whether the substance of the matter is not this: While routine motions may be taken up at this stage, what we have here is not a routine motion. We are now in that part of the daily proceedings, under routine proceedings, which embraces the presenting of reports by standing and select committees, and motions. Clearly a minister or a chairman of a committee can make at this time a motion which would be a routine motion. For instance, there could be a motion for the concurrence in the report of a committee presented to the house, or there could be statements on public matters.
Liberty is taken there, it is true; but by and large they are made under the heading of motions, because if the minister had wished he could make a formal or routine motion and then make his statement under that heading. I do not see how it is possible for anyone to argue that this is a routine motion. This is a motion which would upset the routine. It is a motion which seeks to change the order of proceedings.
I think I know what is in Your Honour's mind. This is a motion dealing with the routine of the house, dealing with the business of the house. I think it is straining the meaning of language to say that it is a routine motion in the sense that the word "routine" is used under routine proceedings. It is a most exceptional motion. It is made once a session at a time when the government considers it to be appropriate. It is not part of the routine business of the house or of the business of government.
It is on that part that I rest my case and ask you to reconsider Mr. Speaker Macdonald's ruling. This is a government notice of motion, it is true, but it is not a routine motion. As a government notice of motion, it can, I submit, under the rules which regulate the conduct of business on Wednesday, be moved only after routine proceedings including routine motions have been disposed of and when the order of precedence covering government notices of motions has been reached. I submit that the argument is sufficiently clear and sufficiently important to ask you to review the previous ruling which you have cited to us.

Mr. Speaker, may I make just one suggestion. You are asked to reconsider a former Speaker's ruling. I think that is a good suggestion. May I say that in order that you may have time to reconsider the ruling, in the light of all the circumstances, the minister should ask the house this after-

Business of the House
noon to give unanimous consent. I think I can say that as far as we are concerned we are prepared to do that. That would give you the opportunity of taking some time to review the question.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON WEDNESDAYS
speechtext:
Perhaps I might put the minds of hon. members at rest by saying that I gave some time to the matter before coming into the house. I considered the ruling of Mr. Speaker Macdonald and also the methods which have been followed in the past with respect to motions presented under routine motions. Motions affecting the business of the house are moved under "motions", which in turn is under routine proceedings.
I have come to the conclusion that the ruling by Mr. Speaker Macdonald was a sound one. That is why I was prepared to give it so quickly and why I had before me the authorities which I cited, namely, the two former rulings of Mr. Speaker Macdonald. Hon. members can rest assured that had I not given it my full consideration I would have been very pleased to delay consideration of it and perhaps give a ruling at a later stage. Every day before the house meets I try to do my homework.
The hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) and other hon. members must realize that I do not feel bound by the rulings of my predecessors. I do not feel absolutely bound to accept all the rulings which have been made by my predecessors. If I find that in my opinion a ruling is not a sound one I shall be glad to consult with my experienced colleagues in the house and change the ruling if in my opinion it is not a sound one for the conduct of the affairs of the house.
I am sorry to say to those who do not accept my view that I have considered the matter and I think the ruling is sound. Rulings of a Speaker are not supposed to be debatable. I allowed the hon. member for Kamloops to speak because I invited him to do so, and I also allowed the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar to speak. I thank them for their observations but I think we should now consider the matter settled.

It is my view that we are dealing much more with the practice of the house at the moment than with a point of order.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in speaking to the motion I quite realize that hon. members, particularly hon. members opposite, may feel that it is preventing them from bringing before the house during the session the motions which are on the order paper in their names; but that does not mean that they cannot discuss the particular subject on which they have given notice to the house, because I fancy there is hardly one subject that cannot be raised on the estimates at one time or another. For that reason there is not, in my opinion, a tremendous cause for concern that their opportunities are being curtailed. As a matter of fact, sir, I have been looking at the records since 1949 and I find that in that year there were 6 private members' days; in 1950 there were 9; in the special session of 1950-51 there were none; in 1951 there were 7; in the second session
Business of the House
of that year there were none; in 1952 there were 8; in the past session there were 6; and we have had 7 so far in this session. Therefore, I feel we are not in any way departing from what has been the practice in the past.
May I add by way of information that, as hon. members know, there are about 18 bills and motions of one kind or another on the government side of the order paper. There are in various stages of preparation about 30 additional bills which will be brought before the house, and the house is quite aware of the fact that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) will be introducing amendments to the Bank Act for special consideration by the banking and commerce committee. There will be other bills of a similar nature that will go to that committee and we have a good deal of business before us now. It does seem to the government that if there is any purpose at all in meeting here in November it is that we should complete the session some time before July 1, or at some such date, as has been usual in the past.
For this reason, and bearing in mind the business which will still have to be dealt with by parliament, we are suggestiing this would be the best course to follow under the circumstances.

speakeroldname: Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):

Mr. Speaker, we now have before us the motion which, of course, we can discuss and on which we can explain the reasons why we approve or do not approve. I do not intend to refer to any of the comments that have been made in regard to the precedure itself. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that much more is involved in this motion than is ordinarily the case.
We have been discussing in this house for some days the importance of making it possible for private members to give full and unrestrained service, and the argument which has been presented in support of the substantial increases, not only for the hon. members of this house but for others as well, is that there should be no restriction on the opportunities open to hon. members to serve in this house their constituents and the people of Canada.
There are on the order paper a number of very important motions, motions which represent the one right, the one opportunity, which many private members will have at any time to place before this house subjects they believe should be given consideration. Unless we are to receive the cynical reply

Business of the House
that arguments do not mean anything anyway, and that there is no use placing motions or private bills before this house-which I hope will never be said-then in that case it must be assumed that the government as well as hon. members on the other side are prepared to give consideration to motions or bills placed by private members on the order paper.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that when so many arguments are being made in regard to the important services rendered by private members, which call for such an increase in the allowances, this is the very time when these private members who have supported these increases should stand up in this house and vote against the motion which denies private members their rights.
The issue in this motion is not an issue merely of the surrender of private members' rights this afternoon. It means the end of any regular debating day on private members' motions and bills, which it has been accorded to have been the practice for some considerable time.
The minister who has spoken in respect of this motion has said that in the last session there were 6 private members' days, and that this year there have already been 7. Mr. Speaker, the fact that the government used the axe so early last year is no argument in favour of hon. members permitting that axe to be used now when these hon. members have emphasized their own importance as private members in this house in the way they did by the vote yesterday.
I repeat that the members who should vote against the axe on private members' rights are those who by their vote have sought to place such high importance on the position of private members in this house. This is a chance for private members who believe in the rights of private members to assert their position and to say that whatever may have been the practice in the past, that will not be the practice now, when members are being provided with allowances which more adequately, at any rate, will compensate them for the time they spend here. If it should take a few days longer-and there can be no suggestion that it would be more than a few days longer, because this is only a part day-still that would be simply a slight justification for the speed with which so many members were prepared to deal with this subject already under discussion without the kind of inquiry some of us thought should be made.
Mr. Speaker, I rose to make a suggestion to the minister, and your ruling has in no way precluded my right to repeat that suggestion.

There are various proposals the minister can make if, for any reason, he attaches special importance to this debate proceeding this afternoon. He can do that without passing this resolution which does away with private members' rights on Wednesday for the rest of the session. I do not want to pick out particular motions or bills without admitting immediately that all motions and bills put forward by private members deserve equal consideration. However, I will say that amongst the private members' motions which have been on the order paper for some time, and in regard to which there has been no opportunity for a debate, is that by the hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Murphy) which appears as item No. 6 under notices of motions. That motion dealing with the extremely important subject of research and the encouragement of research has received editorial support from one side of the country to the other and from speakers not of any one political party but from those associated with business and other activities of various kinds; there has been active and vigorous support for this motion.
I submit that this is the kind of motion that private members should be permitted to bring before the house, and that it is the kind of motion the government should welcome so that they could hear arguments by men and women who have been studying a subject of this kind and as a result, out of the suggestions made, possibly formulate plans which might not otherwise have been considered.
I hope the government will not suggest to us that private members can make no useful suggestions which they themselves have not already thought of. If they were to take that position it would surely be strangely inconsistent with the arguments which have been made in support of other measures still before this house for consideration. No; the government must, in view of the argument they have been making, support the argument that they believe that private members have an important place here and that private members have much to contribute. They have been urging that private members have plenty of time to devote to the study of problems and, presumably, to the making of suggestions here in this house which will help the government. These motions, the private bills or the public bills are not put forward merely for the personal satisfaction of any individual member. They are put forward here as part of the legitimate and proper business of this house.
No matter what number of days have been
permitted in the past before the axe fell,
with the arguments now being made as to

the importance of private members, this is the time to change the trend and to get back to a position where private members in this house are afforded the opportunity to assist the government by placing before parliament suggestions which are in keeping with the status of members as emphasized by the Prime Minister (Mr, St. Laurent) in his remarks in this house on at least two occasions.
When the minister says that any subject matter that is on the order paper can be dealt with on a motion by way of amendment when there is a motion that Your Honour leave the chair when we are going into committee of supply, may I point out to the minister and to hon. members just what that argument implies. That argument implies that these notices of motions, public bills and orders do not really mean much anyway. It implies that this is just so much eyewash and that if anybody has anything to present to this house he might just as well wait until we are going into supply when an amendment can be presented.
Mr. Speaker, that does not meet the situation. Hon, members of this house know perfectly well that while a number of motions may be made by way of amendment as we go into supply, it is not possible to present the number of motions that would correspond to the number of notices of motions, public bills and orders that are put on the order paper of this house. If the argument of the minister means anything at all, it means that private members' proceedings are really very unimportant anyway; that, once we have gone through the motions, we had better dispose of them as soon as possible and let the government, in its might, majesty and power, proceed to steam-roller the business of the house; and that we should then just seek the crumbs that are offered by way of amendments at some later time.
Mr. Speaker, I am using words that I hope will leave no doubt about my belief that what is now being done is utterly inconsistent with every argument made in this house in support of measures that have been presented to this house, one of which was voted on yesterday. I think it would be highly desirable that the minister should not proceed with this motion. There are before us notices of motions on important subjects. There are before us notices of motions that will call for useful debate. There are public bills and orders to be dealt with. Those can be dealt with if we proceed. So far as bills or notices of motions that have come up earlier in the session are concerned, there have been certain occasions when the v/hole hour at the end of the afternoon was not taken because there was an understanding with some members of the government that for reasons of public policy it was not desirable at that point to proceed with either the notice of motion or the bill. I do not need to identify the motions or bills because the government is well aware of those to which I refer.
I do believe that this is a subject with which we can deal in a manner that will be satisfactory to everyone. The bill that will be discussed, if this motion passes, is one presented by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent). I can well understand why members of the government would wish the Prime Minister to be here while that measure is under discussion. There is a way that can be done, namely, to treat the motion before us simply as a motion to deal with government business this afternoon and not deal with any other Wednesday hereafter. I have not been able to consult the other hon. members of my own party but I personally believe that there would be every willingness and desire to deal with this matter by way of a special procedure this afternoon, when the Prime Minister will still be here, as long as the motion is not one which ends private members' days on Wednesdays. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe):
That the motion be amended by striking out the words "and every Wednesday thereafter to the end of the session."

Business of the House

subtopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON WEDNESDAYS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall be very brief in what I have to say. Although I am sorry the motion has been brought forward at this time, I do not think I would have anything to say if it were not for the arguments used by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Harris) in support of the motion.
There is another reason I rise at this time; that is to protest the seeming impatience of private members on the government side of the house to finish the business of the house and get away from here as quickly as possible. Apparently what we did yesterday, and what I have no doubt we will finish in a few moments, has not made any difference in the world to them. All the time they spend here is spent against their will. They are impatient and everything that members on this side try to say is met with boos and jeers in an attempt to shut us off. It is time that private members on the other side of the house were set aright by someone in authority in the government.
The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration said that there was hardly an item in the name of a private member under notices of motions that could not be discussed on other occasions. If that is a valid argument, then surely it is a valid argument against having any private members' days at all. Why have any private members' days if we can discuss these matters on other occasions? There are other occasions on which we can discuss such items. One such occasion is on a motion to go into supply, but opportunities on such occasions are weighted very much in favour of the official opposition. Perhaps there should be some weight in that regard so far as the discussion of grievances and introduction of amendments on a motion to go into supply is concerned.
Take the notices of motions on the order paper today, which we would be debating if this motion were not before us. The first three items are in the names of members of the Social Credit group. I am sure that it is unlikely they would get very many chances during the session to discuss these matters on a motion to go into supply, but a notice of motion gives them an equal chance with the other parties.
The minister also said that we were going to try to finish our business so that we could get away from here some time before the first of July, or early in July. That was the old story before we were made $10,000-a-year men, before we were put on a monthly salary basis. From July to October is a period of four months, which is a pretty long vacation. That is one of the fringe benefits that members
fMr. Drew.]
of parliament receive, but it is out of line altogether with any of the fringe benefits that trade unions get.
I believe we are setting a bad example when we ask for such a fringe benefit for ourselves. There are a great many other fringe benefits which we get, but I will not touch on them today because this is not the time to do so. I regret that I did not refer to them before. As a matter of fact some members have the fringe benefit of nonattendance and still get their indemnity, or whatever you want to call it.
For these reasons I do not think the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration has offered any valid argument for dispensing with private members' day. I realize it is desirable that the house should proceed with the business on the order paper in the Prime Minister's name, and if a request for that by unanimous consent had been made I certainly would have agreed. But that has not been done. The motion was moved, and in my opinion the minister has not supported it by any valid argument.

subtopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON WEDNESDAYS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not minimize the importance of private members' days, but I must say that I was extremely disappointed the other day because I was prepared to speak on two questions that I thought were coming up. You, Mr. Speaker, called the whole list but not a private member rose to speak. As a result we reverted to government business. I know that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) has given a partial answer for this, but I do not see how cabinet ministers can get in touch with every private member who has a resolution on the order paper. As I say, I was disappointed because I thought that private members who had such resolutions on the order paper were making light of private members' day.

subtopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON WEDNESDAYS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not blame you for seeing the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) because we always know that he is to be regarded as a one-minute man. But may I say that, according to the ethics of our procedure in the house, we of this group usually follow our friends of the C.C.F.
We are opposed to this motion, Mr. Speaker. I agree with what the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Maclnnis) has said in respect of members now being on a little different basis. I do not know whether government business that is on the order paper is particularly urgent. Some of it may be. Some of it they may want to have passed at this session, so that we can wind up at the

end of May or June. But much government business is not particularly urgent for a month or two months, or even a year. And I do not see that private members should be crowded out.
Then, there is another principle that has disturbed me for many years. Are we to regard private members' resolutions and bills, and the sort of thing that we consider on private members' days, as merely formalities, merely an opportunity for us to expound as we wish on some resolution? Is that all it is? If that is all, then we might as well dispense altogether with private members' days.
The government may say, "Well, we have certain business that must be done. It is important to us." But what is introduced by private members is just as important to them as government business is to the government.
I do not believe private members' days should be withdrawn at all. However, we like to be accommodating, and if the government wishes to consult with these members in whose names notices of motions stand- and I am referring to Mr. Low, Mr. Quelch, Mr. Hahn, Mr. Maclnnis, Mr. Anderson, and so on-and suggest to them that perhaps they might very well withdraw their resolutions, we would like to be as accommodating as we can. If the motion before us is one of accommodation, we are not going to stand in the way of it. But on a matter of principle, we do not believe private members' days should be withdrawn.

seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that we are in danger of drifting into a very unfortunate position. As I understand it the situation is this. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) has fully recognized the desire of the government to deal with certain business this afternoon. None of us wishes to inconvenience the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) or the government unnecessarily, and to that end the Leader of the Opposition made a proposal a short time ago which, to me at any rate, seemed constructive and co-operative. I was glad that he made it.
But it seems to me there must be two sides in co-operation, and it does appear that what is happening now is simply a case of 83276-110i

"heads I win, tails you lose". We have made a proposal. If it is an impossible one, then surely the reasons for its being impossible might have been outlined. I did not hear them outlined; I understood they were just tacitly refused.
As I say, we wish to help. On the other hand, when I read these notices of motions- and I shall not detain the house to read them in detail, although I have looked through them-it does seem to me that many of them are matters of importance, not only to those who put them forward but to all kinds of people in Canada. And unless some sign of co-operation is shown, it seems to me we are now left-and I am putting it mildly- with precious little opportunity for these to be presented.
The leader of the house has suggested that they might be presented in bits and pieces, here and there, on other occasions, but not on the occasions which we are now asked to give up. I feel very strongly that this is an occasion where sensible men ought to be able to find a reasonable method of co-operation, and I do feel that my leader has made a suggestion which seemed to me to be a reasonable one, but which has not met with response.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON WEDNESDAYS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to say a word on the amendment of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) and in doing so to make a suggestion to the government which I hope will receive favourable consideration.
At the moment we have before us, in the motion and the amendment, two extremes that are quite wide apart. The motion would call for the abolition of all private members' Wednesdays, starting today, and the amendment suggested the possibility that no other private members' days be taken away, with the exception of today.
The suggestion I offer for the consideration of the government, by way of a compromise and as an alternative to the one proposed by the Leader of the Opposition, is that today be made a government day, but that private members be given, let us say, the next two Wednesdays. Maybe the government will beat me down to one, but even that would be a compromise. Someone has suggested that I have to ask for two in order to get one.
It seems to me something like that should be considered by the government. I listened with interest to the statistics adduced by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Harris). I too was doing my homework before I came in here today, and I knew that those were precisely the statistics he would bring in. But what does it prove? He

Business of the House states that in certain sessions we had only a certain number of private members' days. In the years when I first came here there were sessions when we did not have any private members' days at all.
But surely the situation has changed. It might be well for us to look back into the early days of our parliamentary history- away back into the last century, when private members' days continued much longer in the sessions than has been the case in the twentieth century, so far as this parliament is concerned.
I respect the Prime Minister's desire to have today as a government day. He no doubt knows I will vote against the measures that will probably be brought on if this becomes a government day. That being the case it is not my desire to facilitate the bringing on of those measures. On the other hand I respect his desire to have those measures dealt with while he is still here. They stand in his name, and there is a certain amount of responsibility that goes with them. It appears to me that he does not want to go off on his world tour leaving to someone else the responsibility of piloting his legislation through the House of Commons, particularly because of the nature of it.
Therefore because I respect the Prime Minister's sense of responsibility in connection with these bills, even though I am opposed to them, I for one am prepared to accommodate the government so that this would be a government day. However, I do ask that the government consider letting us have another couple of Wednesdays as private members' days.
At the moment I am not saying how I will vote on the amendment offered by the Leader of the Opposition, because I hope that my conciliatory proposal might lead to a suggestion from the government side which would be generally acceptable to the house.

dietitian. Food purchases are paid for from mess funds. Based on the average cost of meals, a rate is struck from time to time and the mess funds are reimbursed from public funds. maintopic: ADVANCES ON CRAIN IN APPROVED FARM STORAGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in moving this
motion I am not advocating that farmers should be paid storage for grain stored on the farm; I am merely suggesting that loans should be made to farmers against grain that is stored on the farm. I mention that fact because there seems to be some misunderstanding in the minds of hon. members regarding what is meant by the terms of the resolution.
It is interesting to note that the subject matter of this motion has been supported by a number of western farm organizations. In order that there may be no misunderstanding on that point I should like to quote from a memorandum submitted by the interprovincial farm union council to the government in November, 1953, as follows:
We would therefore recommend that immediate consideration be given for arranging, through the Canadian wheat board, for cash advances on farm-stored grain.
The recommendation then goes into further details with regard to interest. I might point out that the interprovincial farm union council represents farm unions in British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba. Then there is also a recommendation made by the Saskatchewan wheat pool delegates in annual meeting. I quote one recommendation as follows:
To bring into effect a plan of interim farm financing which will enable farmers unable to deliver grain at country elevators to secure cash advances against grain in store on the farm.

I find it necessary to quote from those statements by those farm organizations because I know there is an impression in the minds of some hon. members that farm organizations in western Canada are not favouring the subject matter of this resolution. No doubt that arose in part from a certain letter written to hon. members by Mr. Marler. However, I think Mr. Marler made it quite clear at the annual convention of the association in Alberta that he is not opposed to farm loans being made if the situation should arise where they were necessary. I should like to quote from an address he made to the convention as appearing in the Alberta Wheat Pool Budget of December, 1953, as follows:
At the present time the federation is not asking the government to back loans on this grain but if the wheat board payments presently being distributed, deliveries which farmers are unable to make and normal credit facilities do not meet the needs of the farmers, the federation is prepared to pursue the matter.
That shows quite clearly that he has quite an open mind on the matter. If the occasion should arise when they consider that farmers do need this assistance, they would be prepared to support it.
I am going to confine my remarks on this matter to four points. First, are the grain growers of western Canada in need of this assistance? Second, is the wheat board the best agency to handle it? Third, is the present situation merely a temporary one, something that may clear up in the near future? Fourth, the need for a long-term farm production program which, if adopted, would require action of this kind.
Coming back to the first point, whether or not the farmers are in need of the type of assistance proposed by this motion, I am not suggesting for one minute that there is a crisis. I admit quite frankly that in my opinion the majority of farmers in western Canada are not in need of assistance. I am speaking mainly about Alberta; I am not in a position to speak about Saskatchewan.
The reason they are not in need of assistance is that there have been three large crops. As a result of having harvested the first two crops they have been able to build up a reserve and are able to use that reserve at the present time to meet the cost of their farm operations. But while I say that, I would also stress the fact that there are at least two groups of farmers who are not in that fortunate position and who represent a considerable number of farmers.
In the first group are those farmers who have suffered one or two crop failures in the past three years. As most hon. members from the west know, there have been some
Grain
areas which have been heavily hailed during the past three years. The farmer who suffered a crop failure in 1951-52 or in 1952-53 has had to use any reserve he had in order to meet his obligation. Hence he has not those reserves available to help meet the cost of operating his farm at the present time. For that reason he is in need of more money, money that would be available if he were able to sell his whole crop.
In the second group I would place what might be called the new farmers, those who have been in operation only since the end of the second world war. Among those I would place returned soldier veterans who have settled under the Veterans Land Act. I think most hon. members are aware that the veteran who settled under that act was able to get only $6,000. He might have had $1,000 or $2,000 of his own, so at the best he would not have more than $8,000.
I think we all agree that to start farming today is quite an expensive operation. A good half-section of land will cost in the neighbourhood of $12,000, or a three-quarter section not quite so good will cost around the same amount. In order to equip that land with a modest line of machinery you would need in the neighbourhood of $8,000. So to start operations on a farm today requires a $20,000 investment.
Under the Veterans Land Act people can get only $6,000. Therefore a man is placed in the position that he has to go into debt to various institutions in order to acquire the machinery he needs for the farm and in *order to increase his land holdings. Consequently, when farmers do have a good crop they have to use the return on that crop in order to repay some of their obligations, or for the purpose of investing in the farm. Men in that position are hit very hard when they suffer a crop failure or when we have a situation such as exists today, where they are not able to sell the whole of their crop.
In addition to the farmers I have mentioned we have the small businessmen who, in many of the smaller towns, act as the farmer's banker. They help to finance his farm operations; they allow him to build up a store bill; they allow him machinery repairs on time, and they allow him to charge his fuel. Consequently, when farmers are unable to sell their crops these men in many cases have to carry these debts on their books for a considerable period of time, and in some cases it puts them in a very difficult position.
On the other hand, I am not suggesting for one moment that the farmers who do not

Grain
need this assistance would apply for it. The only farmers in need of assistance would be the type I have referred to.
On the second point, as to whether or not the wheat board is the best agency to handle advances of the type I have mentioned, it is interesting to note that the interprovincial farmers' union has suggested that the wheat board would be the logical organization to handle them. There are a number of reasons why I feel the wheat board would be the best agency to handle a policy of that kind. In the first place it will be remembered that the wheat board has agents at all delivery points. At many of these delivery points there are no banks. In many cases you will find delivery points 40 and 50 miles from the nearest bank. Therefore the local elevator agent has a far better understanding and knowledge of a farmer's circumstances, the amount of crop he may have harvested, or the amount of crop he will have on his farm, than would a banker who might be 40 or 50 miles away.
Another point it is well to remember is that prior to the time we had the wheat board, it was a common practice in western Canada for the local elevator agents to make advances or loans to the farmer against grain which he had in storage in the elevator. Let us go further and suggest that these advances and loans could and should be made against grain held in storage not in the elevator but on the farm, provided it is a suitable type of storage.
I am not suggesting that loans should be made against grain piled in heaps in the fields. That might mean a substantial loss, although I understand no such loss has been suffered in the past. The reason I use the term "approved farm storage" is that if a motion of this kind were adopted then it would be the wheat board which would lay down specifically the type of granaries in which grain could be housed and on which loans could be made. It would only mean specifying the type of building which would be required to protect the grain from the elements, from livestock, and to a certain extent from theft.
The next point I would like to refer to is the fact that all commercial wheat has to be marketed under permit. Therefore the wheat board agent would be in a position to make deductions against deliveries of grain as they came in for the purpose of repayment of loans. For that reason I would point out that there would be very little danger of the wheat board suffering any loss under a proposal of this kind. There is no comparison between this proposal and the

policy we had in operation a year or so ago, when loans were made against wheat standing in the fields. There was a great deal of risk in that. No one knew whether a crop standing in the fields and which had to go through the winter would ever be harvested, and many people I believe were surprised that losses were not greater. In so far as this motion is concerned I would say there is practically no danger of any loss being suffered providing the local agent exercises his right to demand that early deliveries of wheat be used for repaying loans.
In the motion I have not suggested what the amount of the loan should be. I believe that should be left to the discretion of the wheat board. I notice that in a brief submitted by the interprovincial farmers' union they suggest $1 a bushel, on 15 bushels to the acre. That in my opinion would not be altogether satisfactory because in some districts the total yield might be only 15 bushels an acre or less, and I feel that as a safeguard it would be better to say, using the figure of $1, $1 a bushel up to a certain percentage of the total yield. That would allow for any error in estimating what the total crop had yielded. Therefore instead of saying 15 bushels per acre I think it would be far better to say a certain percentage of the yield per acre.
It is interesting to note that in the United States a policy along these lines has been in operation for a number of years. I believe in the United States it is called sealed storage, but at any rate under this policy advances or loans are made against grain held on the farm in sealed storage. That matter has been brought to my attention on many occasions by farmers in western Canada, who wanted to know why if this was considered sound in the United States where the policy had been followed without causing any heavy loss, a similar policy could not be carried on in this country. I told them that personally I thought it could be carried out here, but it was a question of government policy.
On the third point I would like to pose the question whether the present situation is merely temporary, one that will disappear as soon as we have one or two crop failures. My answer to that question would be that the present situation definitely cannot be considered a temporary one, but rather a recurring one. Perhaps if we had a crop failure next year or the year after these surpluses would disappear, but it is almost just as certain that we are going to have big crops in the future; and while this congestion of today may disappear in two years it is quite possible it may recur four or five years from now.

I can recall many occasions during the past 30 years when we have had congestion at local elevators, and many occasions when farmers have not been able to sell their wheat. This is what happened when local elevator agents received two or three cars at the shipping point. The elevators would open one bin, but of course they could not mix the wheat in that bin. The elevator companies might decide to only take No. 3, with the result that those farmers who had No. 1 and No. 2 wheat and who desired to sell that wheat would have to take No. 3 grade, or not be able to sell it at all. That is what happened in western Canada every time there was congestion under a system of this kind.
Under this proposal, instead of a farmer having to sell No. 1 or No. 2 for a lower grade he would be able to get advances against his grain, and hold it until there was room in the elevator for his type of grain. That would unquestionably be of great assistance to the farmer.
Another reason I believe the present situation cannot be regarded merely as temporary is, as the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) pointed out some time ago, that owing to the great improvement in our farming operations a dry year will not reduce farm yield to as great an extent as in the past. If we go back 20 or 30 years, when most of us were farming with horses, we find that most of our summerfallowing was done with a plow. In those years it would be the end of July before we got through with summerfallowing. By that time there would be a heavy growth of weeds. A lot of the moisture would have been lost. When those weeds were turned over in the loose open furrow the land dried out. Unless we had an excessive amount of moisture the following year we were almost certain to have a crop failure. As a matter of fact, in circumstances of that kind a farmer would be lucky to get his seed back.
That is not the situation today. With the mechanization of farming and the utilization of large surface cultivators, the one-way disc, the rod weeder and other machines, it has been possible for a majority of farmers to get over their summerfallow early in June, thereby preventing the growth of weeds and also conserving the moisture. I therefore do not think there is as great a danger of the kind of crop failures we have had in the past. There will, of course, be short crops, but they will not be nearly as prevalent in the future as they have been in the past. There has also been a greater utilization of fertilizer.
Grain
On the other point, the need for a longterm production program, the reason I am dealing with this matter is that I feel that if a program of this sort is adopted the need for the motion I have moved will become immediately evident. We all know that successful farming today requires that a farmer produce the largest yield he can of the highest possible quality of grain. For a number of years, as a matter of fact, ever since 1945, the United Nations Organization has been urging that all those nations that are able to expand their production of food should do so. I think all members of this house will agree that the farmers have answered that challenge in a magnificent way until today, as a result of good farming operations, they have built up quite a substantial reserve of food in the form of wheat and many other commodities.
While the United Nations Organization has been urging an expansion of the production of food, unfortunately they have not, at the same time, provided the machinery for getting that surplus food to the nations that need it. Hence today we have people in many places, some holding quite responsible positions, bewailing the fact that we have built up a large surplus of wheat and suggesting that it should be sold at fire-sale prices.
Let me quote just one man as an example. I may say many times I have heard statements similar to this. In the Ottawa Journal, under dateline of November 18, appears a statement by Mr. H. A. Stevenson, the president of Barclays bank, speaking at the annual meeting in Montreal. The article reads in part:
He urged every possible effort be made to dispose of Canada's balance of 800 million bushels of wheat available for export, "even if it means, as it probably will, a big sacrifice in the price".
As I say, that statement could be duplicated many times. I would say that these people cannot have it both ways. They cannot, on the one hand, urge the farmers to maintain their production of food at a high level to feed the starving masses of mankind, and then almost in the same breath suggest that, when they have accomplished that purpose, they should be prepared to make heavy sacrifices as a result of it. It seems to me that argument is entirely illogical.
I therefore feel that it is high time the government announced what is their policy in this regard. Is it the desire of the government that the farmers should produce to meet that great potential market represented by the starving people in many parts of the world, or is it the desire of the government that the farmers should limit their production

Grain
to meet the restricted market, namely that market represented by those nations that are able to pay for their imports in dollars?
I think that is an important point, and one that should be made clear to the farmers before their seeding operations start. If the first is to be the objective, then I think the farmers have a right to expect a guaranteed price. In other words they have a right to expect that the government will not allow that increased production to force the price down. On the other hand, if the farmers are to be advised to produce to satisfy the restricted market, then the farmers in this country would be fully justified in reducing their production in the same way as in the United States. During the last year the farmers there were given the option of maintaining their production at the high present level and having a drop in the support price down to, I think, 50 or 60 per cent of parity, or of restricting their acreage by 25 per cent and receiving 90 per cent of parity. I think everyone will agree that the farmers did the sensible thing. They agreed to reduce their production in order to get a satisfactory price.
I would say that if in this country the government is going to say to the farmers, "you have to produce for the restricted market, otherwise your price will be made subject to the law of supply and demand", then the only sensible thing for the farmers would be to do as was done by the farmers in the United States and reduce their production. But let me point out that we in this group are not suggesting that this is a policy that should be followed. We argue that just so long as hunger exists in any part of the world we have an obligation, along with all other nations which have the ability to maintain production at a high level, to do so in order to help feed those starving people. Otherwise the result well may be revolution.
On the other hand, until the United Nations Organization has provided the international machinery by which the surplus food can be gotten to the people who need it, it locks as though the responsibility will have to rest upon each individual government. I notice that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), speaking before the FAO conference at Rome, said that in so far as Canada was concerned the government intended to carry the surplus partly in the interest of the farmers and partly in the interest of the people of all nations. That being the case,
I do not think we are justified in trying to put too much of the burden upon the farmers because they have done the very thing they were asked to do.

I believe that there are ways in which we can help that situation. I do not want to get into that point too deeply because perhaps I would be getting out of order. However, I would remind the house that some years ago the Canadian Federation of Agriculture made a recommendation which was endorsed by the international federation of agricultural producers, and that based upon that recommendation, the FAO council produced a plan which was known as an international commodity clearinghouse. Unfortunately that plan was turned down.
It is interesting to note that one of the main provisions of the international commodity clearinghouse was that the currency of the importing nation would be accepted in payment for the exports of food. That is what we have been advocating in this house on various occasions, namely that we should be prepared to accept sterling in payment of our wheat sold abroad. I am satisfied that procedure would make it possible to export more of our grain to Europe and other parts of the world.
I want to stress the fact that when we advocated the acceptance of sterling, we were not advocating the acceptance of convertible sterling. If you are going to insist that it must be convertible you might just about as well insist on payment in dollars, because the intention would no doubt be to immediately convert the sterling into dollars. What we suggested was the acceptance of nonconvertible sterling to be used either for the purchase of goods in those countries concerned or for investment in those countries. If that action were taken it would hasten the day of convertibility, because by investing the sterling in a country you would make it possible for the country concerned to balance its payments with other nations.
I am not going to get into that point because I realize that perhaps it might be considered outside the bounds of this motion. Nevertheless I mention it for this reason. If in the future we intend to adopt a policy of maintaining our production at a high level to help satisfy the needs of people in other countries, then the logical thing to do would be to try to build up a reserve to be held in this country in order to offset the danger of a crop failure.
If it is to be the policy to build up a substantial reserve so that in the event of a crop failure we will have food to ship to other nations, then it is only fair to say that the cost of maintaining that reserve should not be placed entirely upon the farmers. If any of that reserve has to be held on the farms because there is not room in the elevators,

then at least a system such as that proposed in the resolution could well be adopted, whereby advances could be made against such grain provided it was properly stored. If we are not going to take action of that kind it seems to me that farmers may be forced to curtail production against their will.
That has been pointed out by all the farm organizations. It has been emphasized at some length by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, and if we do adopt a policy of reducing production then I say we are making a mockery of the principles to which we agreed at the United Nations.
We blame Russia to a large extent for our failure to achieve peace, but I do not think we can blame Russia for our failure to provide machinery by which surplus goods can be supplied to people who need them. Therefore the policy of this group is that we should maintain our production at a high level, that we should provide the machinery by which our surplus production can be made available to the people who need it, and that to the extent that any of these surpluses have to be stored on the farms advances should be made against food so stored so the farmers will not be financially embarrassed.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, speaking very briefly, I should like to support this resolution. I am not going to take very much time in doing so because the major portion of my remarks in the speech from the throne debate consisted of arguments in favour of some form of assistance to farmers who are in need of cash and who are, have been and for some time to come are likely to be unable to deliver the major portion of their crop. The hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) spoke of the percentage of farmers who are in need of some assistance of the type envisaged in the resolution, and he referred to certain classes.
When this matter was the subject of debate previously the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) and others expressed the opinion that the great majority of the farmers of western Canada had enjoyed quite a profitable number of years during and since the war and were not in need of any great assistance. As the hon. member for Acadia pointed out, that is true in a large proportion of cases; nevertheless a considerable percentage of the farmers of western Canada have had difficulty in their farming operations in recent years. They have had bad luck in the way of hail, drought or other misfortunes. I do not know what the percentage may be of farmers in western Canada who are not in a position to continue to finance
Grain
themselves, pay their store bills, feed and clothe their families and finance their next year's farming operations without some form of loans or cash advances, but I would think it would run upwards of 25 per cent. It may be more than that, but I think that might be a fair estimate of the number of farmers who need assistance of this kind.
As was pointed out on numerous occasions before Christmas, the situation is quite bad. The amount of grain that may be delivered was initially three bushels to the acre and is now five bushels, and the minimum was of course 500 bushels for a small farm, now increased, I believe, to 1,000 bushels. Such an amount of grain does not by any means provide sufficient money for the farmer to finance himself, carry on his normal operations and put in his next year's crop. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) said not long ago that he could not indicate how soon an increase in the quota will be put into effect, but I do not think it is going to be very soon. The indications are that no increase will take place for some time, and that by the time the next crop begins to come on there will still be a great deal of grain from last year's crop remaining on the farms.
Without any question there are over 300 million bushels of wheat and hundreds of millions of bushels of oats and barley from last year's crop still in the farmers' hands which they have been unable to deliver to the elevators. With the best possible luck in selling these grains either locally in Canada for feed purposes or abroad for human consumption or for animal feeding, we are not going to be able to sell that amount of grain as far as we can foresee. In other words, when the harvesting of the crop commences next fall there is still going to be a considerable amount of last year's crop in the hands of the farmers. Therefore it looks very much as though it will not be possible to have any delivery quota in many places so far as this year's crop is concerned.
Under these circumstances I think it is absolutely essential that some measure such as is envisaged in the resolution be put into effect so that cash can be provided to farmers who need it in order to meet their current living expenses and carry on their operations.
In addition to a method of this sort, I suggested another method in the speech from the throne debate, which I am not going to revive. Guaranteed loans on the part of the government were suggested as another method. I do not need to point out to the house that the resolution does not involve

Grain
the house voting government funds for the relief of western farmers or anything along that line. The resolution reads:
. . . the government should take into consideration the advisability oi enacting legislation at this session of parliament to provide for a system of approved farm storage under which the wheat board may make advances to farmers on grain held on the farms.
In other words the money out of which loans or advances would be made would be the farmers' own money. I get quite tired of hearing certain members who come from other parts of Canada say, either in the house or in the corridors, "You are asking for another handout to the western farmers". Every time any legislation of this type is sought that cry goes up. I should like to make it quite clear that the resolution involves no demand for any handout from anybody to the western farmers. It is a matter of legislation to enable the wheat board, which is handling the farmers' own money, to use that money in a certain way to relieve distress which I think it is quite apparent is going to exist next fall in the case of a considerable number of western farmers, which exists to some extent at the present time and will certainly be very much aggravated a few months from now.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thought there would be no harm in my getting the floor once because we have had to listen to members opposite hour after hour repeating the same thing over and over again. I felt that for once there would be nothing out of place in somebody being heard from this side of the house. I thank you, Mr. Speaker.

I do not desire to delay the house very long on this matter. I wish to support what the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Harkness) has just pointed out, that in this resolution the government is asked to take action which may cost the farmers a lot of money. It is not going to cost the taxpayers much money. It is going to cost the farmers money because if handled by the wheat board the cost will be taken out of the money for which their wheat is sold.
Two years ago I was inclined to agree with the arguments of the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch), that this method of giving farmers advances on wheat stored on their farms, through the wheat board, was perhaps a very easy way of handling the problem then existing. But it has been pointed out to me since that time by many people that there are large numbers of farmers who have grave doubts whether the wheat board, which is a grain marketing organization, should be asked to handle a system under which farmers who did not want to borrow money would have to pay the losses in respect of those who did borrow, where there were losses. They think the wheat board should be kept as a grain marketing organization and not turned into one to finance farmers in western Canada.
People who took that view took the attitude that the legislation passed by the government in 1951 to guarantee loans through the banks was actually more favourable to the farmers because it guaranteed the advances, and if there were any losses they would be met by the people of the country as a whole, the taxpayers of Canada, and not by the farmers. In the event of a calamity such as we had two years ago it is pointed out that it was fair that the taxpayers should bear their fair share of the risk and the loss, rather than loading it all upon the farmers.
It is not generally realized that the cost of financing the wheat board, the cost of storing our wheat, even the cost of carrying it so it will be available when needed, is taken out of the sale price of the wheat, and is carried by the farmers themselves.
The question is as to how far we should go in loading the cost of any measure which may be desirable on the farmers themselves. I refer to a measure such as financing farmers when they cannot sell their grains. How far should we expect the government to go in shouldering part of that responsibility? So far as I am concerned, as I listened to these arguments I developed some doubt as to whether we should ask the wheat board to enter this

field. It was pointed out to me that to have a system like this would cost a great deal of money for purposes of administration. I am told that in the United States, where they have a system of this kind, the cost of administering the plan, involving inspectors who go around to make sure the grain is still in existence and that it is not deteriorating by reason of being attacked by mites and the like, is very considerable indeed. I am also told that there are great losses through grain being stolen, and disappearing. And of course under a system administered by the wheat board the farmers who were ready to get along in the ordinary way would have to help pay these administrative costs, and would also have to help pay for these losses.
I must admit I am beginning to be very doubtful of the wisdom of putting that burden upon the wheat board, because it has the job of marketing our grain and then paying out what is received from the sale. It is very doubtful if we should place further obligations upon it as a result of which it might lose money, and then people would be in a position to say, "Well, perhaps it is not as successful an organization as it should be". In this way the very existence of the wheat board might be endangered.
This is an argument which has been put forward to me by those who have opposed the measure now advocated by the hon. member for Acadia. I believe the wheat board has done such a good job in the marketing of our grain that its existence should not be threatened. It has saved our farmers hundreds of millions of dollars. I am quite satisfied that two years ago, when we had so much low-grade wheat, had that wheat been pressed upon the market, with no buyers in sight, and had there not been an organization such as the wheat board to buy and hold that wheat until it could be disposed of, the results would have been disastrous. At that time the head of the Saskatchewan wheat pool said that instead of our getting $1 for our wheat we probably would have had to sell it for around 40 cents.
I believe that in this way the wheat board at that time saved the producers of western Canada about a hundred million dollars. And I am satisfied that under present conditions, with an oversupply of wheat on hand, were it not for the co-operation between the wheat board in Canada, the commodity credit corporation in the United States, and the wheat board in Australia, enabling wheat marketing to be done in an orderly fashion, the price would have sunk to a very low level. Past history shows this to be so.

This is a matter of great concern not only to the farmers in Canada but to everybody else, because we know that the first thing leading to the great slump in the thirties was the fall in the prices of primary products. Once the primary products fell in price, farmers and other primary producers lost their purchasing power; and then of course those people who made things to sell to the primary producers were thrown out of work, and we were in the midst of a depression.
So I think anything that in any way endangers the wheat board, any extra obligation placed upon it when it is doing such valuable work not only for the farmers but for all people in Canada, should be looked at very carefully. We should ask ourselves, "Are we asking the wheat board and the farmers to finance and carry an obligation that should be carried by the country as a whole"?
Faced with these arguments, as it was the farmers' own money that was being spent I wondered about the propriety of members of parliament, who were elected to act on behalf of the country as a whole, undertaking to spend the farmers' money. That is exactly what is proposed here. If we passed this resolution and the government decided to set up a system of this kind, conceivably we could run our farmers into terrific losses. If a situation is to be developed under which there may be tremendous administrative costs, and ultimately losses, then it should be carried by the people of Canada as a whole, and not by the farmers alone.
If the farmers decide they wish to run that risk, then that is another matter. I have heard so many differing views on the question that, so far as I am concerned, I do not think I should undertake to say what I believe the farmers really want in the matter. Some say they want it, while others say that on no account do they want it. I have wondered how the government could handle this problem, when it has set up a board to handle farmers' products and everything done by that board is paid for by the farmers. I have wondered to what extent the government should decide everything, according to the decisions of parliament, when the producers who pay the shot have but a very small proportion of the representation. Is there not some other way for the government to ascertain the wishes of the farmers? If their wishes are made clear then I believe that our government, being a Liberal government, would want to carry out the wishes of the people whose money they are administering.

There used to be the idea abroad that people could be sent out to govern other people, and they would make wiser decisions than the people would make themselves. Well, it was found that that did not work with human beings. They wanted to have the right to run their own affairs. They might make the same decision as the irresponsible governor might make, but they would not be satisfied unless it was their decision.
In the long run, if this wheat board is going to continue to operate satisfactorily and not be subjected to attack for making some decision which a large group of producers might not agree with, some way should be found to leave the decision in the hands of the producers themselves, letting the government take the attitude: "We are handling your money; we are handling your product; we want to do exactly what you people wish". If the government could take that attitude it would put the responsibility right upon the people who may pay, and they are the people who should have the responsibility.
It would lead to this situation, Mr. Speaker. If any decision was pressed upon the government there would not be the feeling that if we got this through we would be getting something out of the government. There would be the feeling and the knowledge that if anything was decided that might cost money, they would pay it themselves. It would lead to a greater feeling of responsibility and a greater feeling that it was their board and that they should take all necessary steps to protect it. Farmers would be very alert as to the effect of any decision taken.
If the government, say in a matter like this, were prepared to leave it to the holders of permit books whether or not they wanted a system such as this set up, then they would understand that if they voted for it, it might lead to the setting up of an expensive administrative system. It might lead to tremendous losses; it might lead to the wheat board getting into difficulty on account of the propriety of losing all this money realized from the sale of grain. Then if the government could say to the farmers: "You are the ones who are going to pay for this; you are the ones who should now decide it.

We are ready to handle this as you want it handled", the debate would go on amongst the farmers: Is this good, or not?
The farmers are just as anxious to have the wheat board succeed, to preserve it and have it go on and do good work in the future as it has done in the past, as anybody else. They would be very careful about asking it to do anything that in any way might endanger its sound functioning and the successful carrying on of their business.
