There again the wheat board is being asked to do something other than market wheat, and it should be left to the farmers to decide whether they want it to go into that field of activity. The farmers should decide. If it were left to them they would be very careful to make the decision they thought was in the best interests of the wheat board.
I suggest to the hon. member who moved this resolution that it would have been much better to suggest to the house that we approve the idea of asking parliament to ask the government to consider the advisability of empowering the wheat board to conduct a mail ballot of the grain producers holding permits to ascertain the wishes of such producers in regard to setting up a system such as this, or in regard to paying farm storage, where the same argument would apply. Many believe that to pay for farm storage when grain cannot be delivered is a good thing. I think it is a good thing to pay for farm storage when the wheat board is not ready to take the grain, provided the board is given the right to stop paying it when they want the grain delivered. Those who disagree say it would mean that the small farmer would be paying tremendous storage charges to the big farmer and it would work out unfairly in many other ways. Again I ask; why not leave it to the farmers to decide these things? Let them debate it and decide it among themselves, and then give their views to the government.
I am quite aware of the fact that farm organizations at times think they know for sure what the wishes of the farmers are in such matters. Perhaps they do; but we have recognized, by having a system of secret

ballot, that the sure way of finding out what people want is to let them cast a secret vote as to what they do want. On an important matter such as this, which is perhaps a new departure in regard to the handling of our grain, it should be left to the farmers, by secret ballot, to decide what they want.
Just as an example, I might recall to the house what happened in regard to the handling of oats and barley from Manitoba by the wheat board. It was said by certain farm organizations that the farmers of Manitoba were against the wheat board handling oats and barley. Other people said the farmers were favourable to it. Nobody knew for sure what the farmers really did want. Some of us were rather alarmed when the government of Manitoba decided to hold a plebiscite on the matter, because the position then was that unless all the provinces came into the scheme the wheat board would not handle oats and barley for any of them. We wondered whether the people who said that the Manitoba farmers were against the wheat board handling oats and barley really knew what they were talking about.
You, Mr. Speaker, and hon. members will recall that when the plebiscite was held most people were astonished at the strength of the vote for the wheat board handling oats and barley. I think none of the farm leaders expected such an overwhelming vote in favour of the wheat board handling oats and barley. That was an example of the farmers having certain definite opinions and being glad to express those opinions when they got the chance.
I would ask you, Mr. Speaker, to consider how much surer the government must have felt in going ahead with that plan, when they knew that the overwhelming majority of the farmers wanted them to go into that field. There could be no doubt about farmers wanting them to go into that field, for undoubtedly an even greater proportion of the farmers of Saskatchewan and Alberta wanted them to go into that field than did the farmers of Manitoba. Therefore when the government moved it knew that it had the farmers solidly behind it in the matter.
Similarly, in regard to any of these other matters such as the recognizing of voluntary requisitions, the question of paying for farm storage and an approved system of advances by the wheat board, the government through the wheat board could take a mail ballot of the producers of grain who are going to pay, asking, "Are you favourable to this or not?" If they decide that they are favourable the government can proceed then and feel that if there is any loss the producers have definitely asked for it and they have no right to

blame the government in any way. On the other hand, if the producers say "No, we do not want it", the government is not made to appear to go against the wishes of the people.
Therefore I suggest we should make sure we do what the farmers really want us to do. I do urge the government to consider this idea in regard to the activities of the wheat board. The system I am suggesting would be very useful and would be more certain to lay a solid foundation for the future successful functioning of the wheat board than any system of an advisory board or anything else that could be set up. By this means you would be getting the decision of the farmers themselves. If the farmers themselves felt they were running their own wheat board they would be behind it even stronger than ever.
I feel that the wheat board has proved such a success in putting a solid foundation under western agriculture, in introducing a measure of stability into our western farming operations, that I should like to see the most solid foundation possible put under it. I do not think a more solid foundation could possibly be put under it than to base it upon decisions which are made always in line with the wishes of the people themselves. I would ask that this be considered in regard to this resolution, along with the other suggestions I have mentioned.

An eight-bushel quota will mean about 12 bushels per seeded acre, when many of those farmers have threshed 30 bushels, 35 bushels and 45 bushels per acre, on an average basis.

maintopic: ADVANCES ON CRAIN IN APPROVED FARM STORAGE
speechtext: They are lucky.

maintopic: ADVANCES ON CRAIN IN APPROVED FARM STORAGE
speechtext:
The quota works best down in my hon. friend's constituency of Swift Current-Maple Creek, so that when there is no crop failure you have a chance. But that kind of quota has its drawbacks for farmers who ordinarily farm smaller units
because their land is more productive. Hence there is going to be just oceans of wheat on farms in western Canada this year.
I was saying that farmers feel badly, naturally, when they do not get a crop because of bad weather, drought, rust, grasshoppers, sawfly, hail or the hundred and one other things that can happen to a crop in western Canada; they feel badly about it, but they do not blame anybody. They know that next year the weather may be better and that if they go on, year after year, the weather will improve and the crops will come. But nothing angers a farmer more, in my judgment, than to have grain on the farm, and his pockets empty of money, and be unable to market any of that grain which he has on the farm. More and more farmers are coming into that kind of position all of the time.
Mr. Speaker, I think we as a nation should be mighty glad that we have such a large quantity of wheat, namely 713 million bushels, available over and above domestic requirements, for export and for carryover as of December, 1953. We should be pleased that we have those large stocks of grain at a stage in the world's history when two-thirds of humanity go to bed hungry most of the time. I say we should be doing something as a nation to see that fellow human beings in other parts of the world are properly fed. With the huge carryover of wheat looming ahead and the fact that when other nations see that this wheat will be available for export it cannot help having a deterrent effect on the price, I suggest that the government should establish a strategic reserve of wheat, let us say 300 million bushels, that could be taken out of the ordinary market channels. That reserve should be maintained for export to countries when people are hungry and starvation is rampant; and that reserve should be there in case of the drought that is bound to occur at some time in Canada's future.
I suggest that the government should finance that reserve and not the farmers, as was suggested by the hon. member for Rosthern. The government, the people of Canada, should finance this strategic reserve, which is a reserve in the arsenal of democracy for all Canadians and all the people who believe in our way of life.
I have a further suggestion as to how the benefit of that program can be brought down to the farmers on the farm. If the Minister of Trade and Commerce stands up and says the farmers do not want a loan such as that which he provided for them in 1951, I would say to him, "You are right". If the Minister of Trade and Commerce says there is no great destitution and no great hardship, in

Grain
the sense that people are going without clothes, are starving and so on, I will agree with him again. But I think a producer of food in the world in 1954 should have the right to be able to dispose of that food at a fair value. I say that by an amendment to the Canadian Wheat Board Act, the farmers of western Canada should be given the right, not to get loans-for which they go cap in hand to somebody-on grain they have in storage on their farms, but the right to sell the grain they have in storage on their farms and to keep that grain, if necessary, on the farm.
I think the machinery for that kind of program is already in existence. We have the wheat board. All over western Canada we have elevator agents-thousands of them, who are good operators, working for elevator companies, pool companies and line companies-acting as agents for the wheat board. I say the farmer should have the right to go to his local elevator agent and to say to him something like this:	"Look, John, I
have a 1,000-bushel bin of wheat at home. You have no room to enable you to put it in your elevator, so I want to sell it to the wheat board through you, acting as the agent. I should like you to come out, survey that granary, grade it, test it for dockage, and give me my advance payment". Then there could be a further provision that when the elevator agent ordered the grain hauled out, if there should be a shortage or overage as to amount, dockage and so on, that small variation could then be adjusted. I believe the cost of financing such a program, of making provision for farmers to sell grain on their farms, should be borne by all the people of Canada, because I believe that such a policy is in the interests of the people of this nation.
The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) is leaving tomorrow on a world tour, and I want to join with those who have wished him bon voyage. We wish him happy landings; we wish him success in his important trip; we hope that he will have a safe return to Canada and will be able to give us an interesting and valuable account of his world tour. But, with such a strategic reserve of wheat now in existence, I should like to see the Prime Minister placed in such a position by parliament that when he goes and sees the manner in which people live in the various countries of the world he visits, when he himself sees the hunger, he would be able to say to the governments of these countries that when he returned to Canada he would recommend to his colleagues and to the House of Commons that we take steps to help alleviate that hunger. If Canada would take such a lead I believe

we would make a magnificent contribution to world peace, and it might go down as the greatest single act of statesmanship in.
1954.

maintopic: ADVANCES ON CRAIN IN APPROVED FARM STORAGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not going to speak at length, because I do not wish to talk out this measure. I am sure the house is very anxious to hear the reaction of the minister to the resolution before us, and is also looking forward to an opportunity to vote on this most important question.
Certainly the storage problem has become very serious. There are several hundred million bushels of grain on hand today, and in view of the fact that the storage problem will be a continuing one in the days ahead it becomes necessary to consider whether or not the government should consider the advisability of enacting legislation at this session of parliament to provide for a system of approved farm storage under whiclr the wheat board may make advances to farmers on grain held on farms.
Certainly the storage problem today is a costly one. Recently I asked a question in the house for the purpose of ascertaining what it was costing to store Canada's wheat. The answer given by the Department of Trade and Commerce was that the amount paid by the wheat board for storage of wheat from the 1st of January to the 31st of December, 1952, was $17,043,000 and that during the period from the 1st of January, 1953 to the 31st of July, 1953, the amount was $12,733,000; or, taking the entire period, over $50,000 a day. That amount is increasing and has increased at an accelerated rate during recent years, compared with the amounts paid previously.
Even on the present basis elevator companies are apparently asking for an increase in storage rates. The minister indicates that is not so, but I have a press dispatch here from Regina which reads as follows:
J. H. Wesson, president of the Saskatchewan wheat pool, said it is essential that handling and. storage charges on grain be brought into line with actual operating costs. He told the pool's annual meeting here that handling charges have changed little since 1938, but cost of labour and operating expenses have increased greatly. Under average production with lower volume, present rates would result in a deficit.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: ADVANCES ON CRAIN IN APPROVED FARM STORAGE
speechtext: There is no change in the rates this year.

maintopic: ADVANCES ON CRAIN IN APPROVED FARM STORAGE
speechtext:
The minister says there will be no change in the rates this year, but nonetheless it is apparent that there will be an endeavour shortly to obtain an increase in these rates. Certainly storage facilities have been taxed to the utmost. The plan

envisaged in the resolution before us is the only one I can conceive of which can meet the situation. I do not go as far as to say that storage should be paid on all wheat on all farms; but certainly, subject to reasonable limitations on the total amount of wheat to be stored on a farm, there should be provision for something in the nature of storage payments to be made. Certainly the problem we face is not one for a period of only a few months. Our accumulating surpluses are such that they demand either one of two things, the provision of storage facilities or, alternatively and more satisfactorily, the security of markets for our wheat.
I think the minister might well place before the house something of what is being done to secure markets. I understand that representatives are now or have been in the Far East, and also in Central America and Washington, whose purpose is to endeavour to secure markets. That is a laudable purpose. Is the minister in a position to say whether or not the price at which we hold Canadian wheat today is such as will deny us within the days and months ahead, within the next year or so, sales that otherwise might be available to us?
That brings up a suggestion on which I endeavoured to secure an answer the other day during the course of the debate on foreign affairs. It has to do with markets in the U.S.S.R. What is being done to that end? Is wheat considered a strategic material? Is the minister in a position to say anything more than he said on the 4th or 5th of January, when he was reported to have stated that larger and more extensive trade with the U.S.S.R. was being contemplated? Certainly the Canadian farmer is concerned.
The minister says we are not losing any markets. He says the fact that other countries are growing wheat in excess of their previous production, thereby denying us sales, is not to be considered as a loss of markets. What else is it? We are speaking of markets, the opportunity of selling at a reasonable price, and however that loss is caused it is nonetheless a loss of markets.
I suggest to the minister that he place before the house and country something of the nature of the negotiations that are taking place today. We read about them in the newspapers. In today's Ottawa Journal we read that the British Chancellor of the Exchequer said in their House of Commons that the finance ministers of the commonwealth countries have decided to take advantage of trade with the communist bloc whenever possible. He was reporting to the
Grain
House of Commons yesterday on the finance ministers' conference at Sydney, Australia. He went on to say:
It was agreed that restrictions on trade with China were stricter than those on the Soviet bloc. The finance ministers saw the advantage of extending east-west trade and decided to take advantage of it wherever possible.
Is the minister in a position to say whether, if there is going to be trade, that trade will include wheat and other agricultural products? Those are things the people of Canada want to know. Those are the larger issues that today face the Canadian people in the marketing of their wheat, and in the piling up of these surpluses which are becoming colossal in extent and which must necessarily have a detrimental effect upon prices in the days ahead.
The hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) says, in so far as this problem of storage is concerned let us have a referendum. Well, Mr. Speaker, I do not think that meets the situation. I think members from western Canada have found everywhere in rural constituencies a demand that something be done to compensate farmers for providing suitable storage facilities for the wheat lying on the farms. If the farmer markets it, then storage is paid to the elevator companies, so the situation is no different whatsoever in so far as the final amount the farmer will receive is concerned.
Farm unions have asked that something be done along the lines of what is asked in this resolution. Certainly in those parts of western Canada-northern Saskatchewan, for instance-where there are small farms, there is a pronounced demand even today for something in the nature of loans by the wheat board on wheat in properly accredited storage bins. This debate has made it possible for the minister to give the house facts rather than roseate pictures, and I ask him when he speaks to let the country know what is being actually done in connection with the securing of markets for this surplus.
The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) says, let us give it away and provide assistance to underdeveloped countries. Well, that has its dangers. Today we are fearful that the United States of America is going to dump hundreds of millions of dollars worth of farm products at fire-sale prices in various parts of the world. We want a certain course followed here in order to dispose of our surplus, and at the same time we view with the greatest possible alarm the fact that the United States will do that which some hon. members so glibly advocate as a solution for our problem.

Grain
Certainly there is something to be said for elevating living standards in other parts of the world. I saw that three years ago when I was in the south Pacific. At that time I came back and advocated assistance under the Colombo plan, and I have heard about it ever since. I believe that a reasonable extension of the amount being expended under the Colombo plan-certainly a doubling of the amount that is being expended today-would not be a very heavy load for Canada to carry. That would make $50 million altogether, which would go a long way toward raising the standards in those countries to which the Colombo plan applies.
There are arguments on both sides. I know that Paul Hoffman, the American administrator, said very recently that if between 1942 and 1945 we had expended $500 million by way of assistance to China in agricultural products and the like, China might never have become communist. On the other hand we must realize that we live in the world of today; and if we in Canada, in order to get rid of our surpluses, embark upon such a policy as some advocate, a policy of gifts or of selling at reduced prices in order to assist countries in other parts of the world, we will find ourselves criticized in the United States to the same extent that we in our own country today fear the danger of the United States doing that very thing.
I would like the minister to explain what is being done. We have learned from Mr. Butler, the Chancellor of the Exchequer in Great Britain, what is being done over there. We know something of what is being done about surpluses in Australia. We ask our minister to let the house know the policy of the government with respect to east-west trade, and to what extent, if any, the tremendous surpluses we have in Canada will ultimately find markets, either through east-west trade or through trading with other countries of the world.

maintopic: ADVANCES ON CRAIN IN APPROVED FARM STORAGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to be permitted a few minutes in this debate on the subject of advances on farm-stored grain. I can assure the house that I shall not take more time than was taken by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue), who is so anxious to have a vote on the matter. I shall try to discuss it within the same time limit, and also from the point of view which I suggest holds the greatest interest of farmers in western Canada.
I refer to the effect of advances on farm-stored grain, or the effect of any other measures that may be proposed in connection with farm operations or farm financing

upon ultimate wheat board operations in western Canada. I refer to the effect it would have upon an organization the farmers in western Canada have spent almost all their lives in building up and bringing to the point where it has become the selling agency for the grain produced by those farmers.
I have been farming since 1916; and I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that the farmers I know are not going to be parties to any arrangement that would have a detrimental effect upon the wheat board. And I say that if any other member in the house does not take the same stand, then he is doing a disservice to western Canadian farmers. We are not going to spend all our lives building up an institution that has been of such great benefit, as the wheat board has been, and then proceed to enact some measure which will have the effect of destroying it.

maintopic: ADVANCES ON CRAIN IN APPROVED FARM STORAGE
speechtext: Do you not trust your government?

maintopic: ADVANCES ON CRAIN IN APPROVED FARM STORAGE
speechtext: You don't apparently.

maintopic: ADVANCES ON CRAIN IN APPROVED FARM STORAGE
speechtext:
We have been operating under the wheat board for a number of years. It has done a magnificent job as a selling agency, the most magnificent of any similar agency anywhere in the world. It has done the job under difficult conditions. We have to export more of our grain than any other country in the world. In other words we in Canada, with 1 per cent of the world's population, are producing 7 per cent of the world's supply of wheat. If anyone knows of any other country carrying on with the same success, then I have not heard about it thus far.
Our wheat board has been selling wheat. We now are faced with a situation in which the government is asked to provide that the wheat board can lend the farmers' own money back to them by way of advances on approved storage. Those with approved storage facilities would be eligible for advances. What about it if any losses should be sustained? Are the farmers going to be asked to pay them? I do not know very many farmers who are going to be willing to accept losses caused by some other farmer's inability to repay the advances.
In that connection we have had the experience of the British wheat agreement, and we have had the experience of the $65 million wheat payment to western farmers. I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that if the people of this country are going to be called upon to pay any losses in connection with western wheat through the operations of

Grain
the wheat board, then that will be the end of the wheat board. I believe I am correct in saying that.
Why do I say that? I say it because not more than 7 per cent of the people of Canada want the wheat board. Are we living in a democracy, or are we not? If we are, then we are dependent upon the rest of the people of Canada; we are dependent upon how they advise their members to vote. If we are only 7 per cent of the people of Canada who want the wheat board, then we are in this position. After all, it is only the farmers of Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Alberta who want it, and not all those farmers. I do not know of anyone in British Columbia that wants the wheat board. I do not know of many east of the great lakes that want the wheat board. I do know of a large number of people who might be satisfied to have no wheat board.
I say that not more than 7 per cent of the people of Canada want the wheat board. But our socialist friends ignore that entirely. They say that the government should operate this system irrespective of the wishes of the rest of the people of Canada. I would tell every person in Canada that the Liberal members of parliament over the years have been protecting that wheat board and have made it operative.

maintopic: ADVANCES ON CRAIN IN APPROVED FARM STORAGE
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question?

maintopic: ADVANCES ON CRAIN IN APPROVED FARM STORAGE
speechtext: What is worrying you?

maintopic: ADVANCES ON CRAIN IN APPROVED FARM STORAGE
speechtext: Is the hon. member in favour of the coal subsidies?

maintopic: ADVANCES ON CRAIN IN APPROVED FARM STORAGE
speechtext: Well, what has that to do with an organization that has been set up on behalf of the western wheat growers?

maintopic: ADVANCES ON CRAIN IN APPROVED FARM STORAGE
speechtext: What has your speech got to do with it?

maintopic: ADVANCES ON CRAIN IN APPROVED FARM STORAGE
speechtext:
The coal subsidy is not a permanent affair. In any event, I am saying that the overwhelming proportion of the people of Canada are, to say the least, uninterested in the wheat board of this country. Perhaps it is our duty to subsidize the coal miners and even the gold miners. Saskatchewan has a few subsidies, but I have not time to go into that now.
In any event, those things are temporary. We are supposed to be on a permanent basis in connection with our wheat operation. That was the argument when the British wheat agreement was discussed in this house. Everyone in this House of Commons agreed with that wheat agreement. Was not 83276-111
that the basis upon which the wheat agreement was discussed? All hon. members in the house were in favour of it.
Then, after the wheat agreement with the "have regard to" clause in it was not kept, in our estimation, what was the story in this House of Commons? It was not the same at all. None of us was satisfied with the British wheat agreement and particularly our socialist friends, although at the beginning they were in favour of the agreement. Therefore when there were no results, or no payments under the "have regard to" clause, our socialist friends asked the people of Canada to pay $325 million on account of the fact that their socialist friends in Britain would give no consideration to the "have regard to" clause. That was what they asked us to do, and the talk was that the people over in Britain, the socialist government, were telling us here in Canada that our wheat growers were better off than the farmers in Britain, and why should they be taxed to pay us, who were better off? It may be good socialist theory, but it works both ways.
While I am at it I should like to say this. We hear socialist advocates-these give-away gentlemen, some of whom have never produced anything to give away, but who are always willing to give away someone else's production-suggest that we should give away our production. Our socialist friends are so generous with other people's money. They say we should feed the underprivileged people of the world. I agree with them. I do not like to see starvation anywhere. But I should like to point out that if production in this world in the past years had depended upon the socialist system we would not be able to feed the underprivileged people of the world; we would not have enough to feed ourselves, because the socialist system cannot produce. The socialist system is non-productive.
With respect to feeding the underprivileged people of the world, I think the government would be prepared to make an agreement with the socialists and say we would double what they might give; we would give two bushels for every one they give to the underprivileged people on earth. We will match them. Let them give us an example of what the socialist countries have been doing to feed the underprivileged people of the world, and we will match them. In other words we will outdo them. We will give so generously in proportion to what these socialist countries do that they will be put to shame.
I should like to have time to say a few words more about Saskatchewan and about

Grain
the attempts to alleviate the crisis of wheat under the snow. We have heard about crises in Saskatchewan. We have had the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) make the same speech, with the odd change in a word here and there, in 1949, in 1950 and 1951. I think 1950 or 1951 was the year the wheat was under the snow. I never heard anything quite so sad as a speech that was made by that hon. member in that year. According to him the people of Saskatchewan were starving. This government made some provision for them by guaranteeing the banks. Of course the socialists held up their hands in horror when the banks were mentioned. Don't forget, the farmers are going to have to pay interest on the advances from the wheat board, because the wheat board has to borrow that money somewhere and has to pay that interest. That interest will be paid by the wheat board and charged back to the farmers.
I do not know whether it is against socialist theory to have advances. I am glad to get advances made by anyone. I have had quite enough to do with advances, I can tell you that. My trouble has been that I have always had so many cash advances that I have not been in a position later on to cover them. I do not say that all the farmers are in that position, because most farmers are good farmers, but I would not care to say that of myself.
Under the snow cash advances were provided for to the extent of $20 million. Of that $20 million some $635,000 was used to eliminate the crisis that existed out in Saskatchewan at that time. Then along came the foot-and-mouth disease crisis, and we are still feeling the effects of it. The argument of the hon. member for Assiniboia at that time was that the poor farmers out there had lost their herds of cattle through foot-and-mouth disease and the government refused to pay them, or the government would not give them sufficient to cover their losses.
The government, as it always does, took care of those crises as they arose from time to time. At least this government does that. Therefore the government paid these farmers who had losses through foot-and-mouth disease, and I have not heard a complaint from a single one of them. In fact I understand that most of them were tickled to death because they received more for the herds that were lost through foot-and-mouth disease than the market would have given them later on. Then the hon. member for Assiniboia said, "The reason the government paid you is that an election was coming along". Elections are the only things the

hon. member for Assiniboia ever thinks of. That is the only thing he is thinking of now. That is all he ever does. That is exactly what happens. From day to day in this House of Commons he refers to elections.
The government met its commitments under all causes and under all circumstances. Then they talk about the loss of markets. Well, what are the socialists going to do about this? What I should like to know is, what are they going to do about it? They have the standard remedy for everything- give it away. Well, if you took all the wheat that ever grew in this country and gave it to the underprivileged, who comprise about two-thirds of the people of the world, would that be a permanent solution? Would it eliminate communism? It is said that hunger causes communism. I want to know what causes socialism.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

speechtext: Go and look in the mirror.

maintopic: ADVANCES ON CRAIN IN APPROVED FARM STORAGE
speechtext:
It is suggested that payments should be made on approved farm storage. Who is going to approve it? These socialists are always arguing against too many government inspectors, too many people going around the country in the pay of the government investigating other people's business and disturbing them. There are quite a few disturbed people in this House of Commons. I have never attended here without hearing someone saying that he is disturbed. In any event they will continue with that point of view, that while the purpose might be good there would be too many inspectors.
In any event it is not the approved people who need help, I think it is the people who have their grain in places which even the socialists would not approve who need help. In the southwestern section of Saskatchewan there have not been sufficient crops over the years to permit the building up of permanent storage space. As has been mentioned in the house before, I think by the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Jutras), out of every 100 bushels stored outside on the grass of the prairies there would be a loss of 8 bushels.
Working that out on the basis that over the years in southwestern Saskatchewan at least half the time we do not have any crops, we would have to build substantial structures to conform to these requirements, and it is just a little bit doubtful whether it would be a paying proposition. The same thing applies to machinery. You do not hear the university people in western Canada advocating the building of elaborate structures to house machinery, because the investment in those buildings would be greater than the deterioration of the machinery over

a period of years. There would be only a few people in southwestern Saskatchewan who would come within this category. They would have to depend on that storage for the advances that would be made, and therefore they would not be helped. Those are the people I want to help, the people who need it.
I think perhaps some solutions have been offered here today that would fit in. The hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) has made some suggestions. There has been criticism, ridicule and all the rest of it, but we are used to that in Saskatchewan. There is merit in what he said. We used to have the Saskatchewan farm loan board in that province, but that was taken over by the dominion. It was a good thing regardless of what happened to it. The province of Saskatchewan had that board to meet the farm crisis, but it was not continued by the socialists. I am suggesting it was a pretty good farm loan board. The Liberals operated it for quite a number of years.
I would not suggest the setting up of a provincial farm loan board. I suggest that they set up a provincial wheat loan board and make some effort by means of guarantees to the banks through the municipalities, as was done when advances were made during previous years. The municipality was guaranteed by the province, which in turn was guaranteed by the federal government. They operated in western Canada, and over those years about $118 million was distributed.
Perhaps some system could be worked out to provide assistance to those people who could not obtain the approval of any board or any organization or any people. Perhaps we could work out machinery whereby the municipalities could give consideration to applications by farmers, because no one knows the farmers better than the municipal officials. The advances could be made to the farmers on behalf of the provincial government through the banks. After all the farmers have to pay the interest anyway, under any system, and most of these needy people could be helped.
As I was saying a minute ago, in southwestern Saskatchewan it is not the surplus of wheat that causes the crisis, it is the lack of wheat that has been the cause of most of the crises in our country. If we have had crises they have been crop failures. If we are going to have any kind of crisis, I would like to have this kind, with too much wheat. If I had to make a choice, I would like to have a wheat crisis.
If we could have had that kind of crisis throughout all our history in southwestern 83276-llli
Grain
Saskatchewan then we would be in the same category as the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue), who is always talking about the unbearable burden of income tax payments in Saskatchewan. We hear about a group of Saskatchewan farmers who are paying more income taxes than all the people in any other province in Canada, and we are told that those poor people who are paying income taxes should not be paying them. I do not think the hon. member's figures are correct in respect to that. I doubt whether many of his figures are correct.

speechtext: Are you for it or against it?

maintopic: ADVANCES ON CRAIN IN APPROVED FARM STORAGE
speechtext:
I have not much political acumen-whatever that word means; I did not go to school for very long, so I have not the vocabulary of some of these university graduates who went to university to study socialism. If I had it I would say that that kind of crisis is the one that can best be overcome. I think we would suffer less from that type of crisis than from any other that I know of.
When I hear talk about these income tax payments by the farmers of Saskatchewan the only thing I object to is that I am not in the same category. I would like to be in that same group. If all the people of Saskatchewan, including those who could not obtain these approved loans, were in the position of having to pay income tax, many more people in Saskatchewan would be happier than they are. I do not particularly like the income tax situation, but I think the government is trying to make it as fair as it is possible to make that situation. I think if you make a study of it and obtain the actual facts you will have to admit that it is fair.

maintopic: ADVANCES ON CRAIN IN APPROVED FARM STORAGE
speechtext: Are you for or against it?

maintopic: ADVANCES ON CRAIN IN APPROVED FARM STORAGE
speechtext:
It is not one policy for one province and another policy for another province, as was the case with the socialists in Saskatchewan. I have been trying to suggest how we can overcome or circumvent this crisis. I have been suggesting that if there is a crisis-the socialists always have one-the solution should be on the basis of the protection of our wheat board.
As I mentioned at the beginning, every one of us should be doing a service to our people in protecting that wheat board. We should not allow it to get in a position where the other 93 per cent of the people of Canada may say, "The farmers of western Canada do not want this organization". The Liberals of western Canada over a period of many years have done a magnificent job in convincing the other 93 per cent of the people who may be uninterested in the wheat board that it is a good organization.

subtopic: EXPRESSION OF GOOD WISHES ON IMPENDING TRIP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) will not be in the house tomorrow and will not be here for some time, I think it might be appropriate before we leave the house this afternoon to wish him every success on the trip he is making and to repeat what has already been said in this house, that in the good will and friendly sentiments which he will be conveying to the other nations of the common-weath and other countries he will be carrying a message of unanimous good will and understanding from every member of this parliament and from all the people of Canada.
Later this week he will be lunching with the Prime Minister of Great Britain, and I know it will be the wish of many of us that he convey a message of good will to him. Also later, when he goes to France, I know it will be the wish of all of us that with that special aptitude he has for speaking to the people of that great country he assure them of our common concern for the great causes that they are serving at this time.
In every other country he will be speaking, in his expressions of good will, for all the people of Canada; and we wish him well on his trip.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: EXPRESSION OF GOOD WISHES ON IMPENDING TRIP
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on behalf of my leader, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), and on behalf of the members of this group, I wish to join with the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) in saying bon voyage to the Prime Minister and in expressing our very best wishes to him for a happy and useful trip. We are indeed glad to know he is going as Canada's ambassador of good will. We shall follow his trip with interest and await with keen anticipation his report on his return.

subtopic: EXPRESSION OF GOOD WISHES ON IMPENDING TRIP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sorry I was not in the chamber at the moment the Leader of the Opposition rose to


express best wishes on behalf of his party to the Prime Minister. I happened to be out recording a broadcast, and it might be of interest to the Prime Minister to learn that the member of parliament who was recording a broadcast before I arrived-a member of the opposition, incidentally-was telling of the Prime Minister's proposed trip. He did it quite delightfully and concluded by trusting the people of Canada would follow the Prime Minister on his trip.
He might well have added that all the people of Canada wish him the very best of luck. Such is the expression of our democracy. I am sure the members of this group join with other hon. members who have spoken and wish the Prime Minister the very best the Lord God in heaven can give him on this trip. May that include his protection, much pleasure, usefulness, and a glorious and safe return.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was not in the house last Monday when good wishes were extended to the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) on the occasion of the round-the-world trip he will be starting on tomorrow.
However, I did send to him, this very day, a personal letter in which I said that, although we sometimes take divergent views, the member for Quebec West has nevertheless much respect and admiration for the first citizen of this country. On this occasion when he is setting out on a tour around the world, during which he will certainly know how to put clearly the Canadian viewpoint and show other countries how we practise true democracy here in Canada, I want to extend to him, in my own name as well as in the name of the electors I have the honour to represent, my most sincere wishes for a good journey and a happy return. I ask Divine Providence to protect the right hon. Prime Minister, my famous neighbour, from any untoward incident, so that he may come back to continue the work he has so valiantly begun.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: EXPRESSION OF GOOD WISHES ON IMPENDING TRIP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do wish to express very sincere thanks to the Leader of the

Opposition, the spokesmen for the other groups, the hon. member for Quebec West (Mr. Dufresne) and to the hon. member for the county where I had the advantage of spending some delightful weeks during the summer a year ago, for the good wishes they have expressed. I confess I do feel that I have the good wishes of all the people of Canada in undertaking this visit to several countries where, I can assure you, I shall be very proud to be received as an ambassador of Canadian good will.
